p: The Spirit is sent into 'our' hearts in the older text and 'your' hearts in the Byzantine text.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (witness lists as reported by Metzger and the NA28 apparatus; the individual manuscripts were not rechecked here)
readings.plain: into our hearts

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (the Greek behind the KJV)
readings.plain: into your hearts

why: The Plain follows 'our'. It is the reading of the editions built on the oldest manuscripts. It is also the harder reading: after 'you are children' a scribe would smooth the sentence to 'your hearts', while 'our' changes person in mid-sentence. Paul may be including himself and other Jewish believers beside the Gentile 'you' (see the note on 4:6).

a: you are also an heir, through God
t: Heir 'through God' or 'of God through Christ'?
p: Older manuscripts say 'an heir through God'; later ones say 'an heir of God through Christ'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Papyrus 46 (about AD 200) and Codex Vaticanus (300s) among the early manuscripts (Witness lists are those reported by Metzger and the NA28 apparatus; the individual manuscripts were not rechecked here.)
readings.plain: you are also an heir, through God

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'heir of God through Christ')
readings.en: an heir of God through Christ
readings.plain: you are also an heir of God through Christ

why: The Plain follows the shorter, older reading. 'Through God' is odd (Paul would normally write 'of God'), and a scribe would find it easy to fix by writing the familiar 'heir of God through Christ' (Romans 8:17). The longer reading is an easy and natural correction.
b: The sense is nearly the same either way: God is the one who makes the believer an heir. The KJV reader will find 'heir of God through Christ', which echoes Romans 8:17.

a: The test that my body brought you
p: Did Paul's weakness test the Galatians, or was it his own test? One pronoun changes.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (witness lists as reported by Metzger and the NA28 apparatus; the individual manuscripts were not rechecked here)
readings.orig: τὸν πειρασμὸν ὑμῶν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου
readings.plain: The test that my body brought you

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: τὸν πειρασμόν μου τὸν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου
readings.en: my test, the one in my flesh
readings.plain: My test, which was in my body,

why: The Plain follows 'your test in my flesh', the reading of the oldest manuscripts and the harder one. It means: my body was a test for you, a thing you might have rejected. 'My test' is the easier phrase, and a scribe could have changed 'your' to 'my' because it seems more natural for Paul to speak of his own trial.
b: The Plain's 'brought you' tries to keep the unusual 'your test'. The KJV follows the other reading ('my temptation which was in my flesh').

a: So where is that joy of yours now?
p: Two readings of the opening words of 4:15 change a present question into a past one.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: So where is that joy of yours now?

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (the Byzantine also adds 'would' later in the verse)
readings.orig: τίς οὖν ἦν ὁ μακαρισμὸς ὑμῶν;
readings.plain: So what was that joy of yours?

why: The Plain follows 'Where, then, is', the reading of the editions built on the oldest manuscripts. Both readings are ancient, but the difference is small in meaning: Paul is asking what has become of the Galatians' early gladness.

p: A small change of a word: 'children' or the more tender 'little children'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tregelles
readings.plain: My children

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'My little children')
readings.plain: My little children

why: The Plain follows tekna, 'children', which the SBL and NA28 print. The editors who print teknia (the Tyndale House GNT among them) take it as Paul's tender form, used elsewhere (1 John 2:1). The decision is close. Either way, Paul speaks as a parent in labor. The editions are the only evidence reported here; the manuscript support was not rechecked.
b: Paul uses teknia only here, and John uses it often, so some scribes may have been influenced by John. The evidence is mixed.

a: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia.
p: Three forms of the sentence: 'Hagar is Sinai', 'For Hagar is Sinai', and 'For Sinai is in Arabia', with no Hagar.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: τὸ δὲ Ἁγὰρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ
readings.en: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
readings.plain: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia.

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia')
readings.orig: τὸ γὰρ Ἅγαρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ
readings.en: For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
readings.plain: For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia.

readings.w: The Latin Vulgate ('Sina enim mons est in Arabia'); Metzger reports that some Greek witnesses also leave out 'Hagar' (as reported, not rechecked here)
readings.orig: τὸ γὰρ Σινᾶ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ
readings.en: For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia
readings.plain: For Mount Sinai is in Arabia.

why: The Plain follows the text with 'Hagar', the form the major critical editions print (they differ only between 'Now' and 'For'). Metzger's Commentary discusses all three forms. The Greek witnesses for each form were not rechecked here, so this choice rests on the editions. The omission could be a scribe's fix for an odd sentence (a mountain called Hagar?), but how strong its Greek support is has not been established here, so this is less certain than most choices in the letter.
b: If 'Hagar' is not in the original, Paul would be saying only that Sinai is in Arabia, and the link between Hagar and the mountain would come from the context. The Vulgate itself reads this way. The question matters for the sense: it decides whether Paul himself calls Hagar 'Sinai' or leaves the link to the reader.

t: 'Our mother' or 'the mother of us all'?
p: The KJV's 'the mother of us all' is in the Byzantine text, not in the older manuscripts.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Papyrus 46 and Codex Vaticanus among the early manuscripts (Witness lists are those reported by Metzger and the NA28 apparatus; the individual manuscripts were not rechecked here.)
readings.plain: She is our mother.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'the mother of us all')
readings.en: who is the mother of all of us
readings.plain: She is the mother of us all.

why: The Plain follows the shorter text. The longer reading 'of all of us' is a natural expansion, perhaps from the thought of Isaiah 54 or Genesis 3:20 ('mother of all living'), and the older manuscripts do not have it.

a: As for you, brothers, you are children born through the promise, as Isaac was.
p: The older text says 'you are children of promise'; the Byzantine text says 'we are'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles
readings.plain: As for you, brothers, you are children born through the promise, as Isaac was.

readings.w: Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'Now we, brethren, as Isaac was, are the children of promise')
readings.plain: As for us, brothers, we are children born through the promise, as Isaac was.

why: The Plain follows 'you'. The letter has been speaking to the Galatians as 'you' (4:19-21), and the verse that follows addresses them again (4:31 says 'we'). Scribes may have changed 'you' to 'we' to match 4:26 and 4:31. The difference is small.

a: Christ has set us free, to live in freedom. So hold your ground, and do not get tangled up again in a yoke of slavery.
t: A different order and joining of the words
p: The older text is a short statement and a command; the Byzantine text joins them in one long sentence.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.orig: τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ἡμᾶς Χριστὸς ἠλευθέρωσεν· στήκετε οὖν
readings.en: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm, then
readings.plain: Christ has set us free, to live in freedom. So hold your ground, and do not get tangled up again in a yoke of slavery.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free')
readings.orig: τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ οὖν ᾗ Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἠλευθέρωσεν, στήκετε
readings.en: Stand firm, then, in the freedom with which Christ has set us free
readings.plain: So hold your ground in the freedom that Christ has given us, and do not get tangled up again in a yoke of slavery.

why: The Plain follows the older text, in which the first clause stands alone: 'for freedom Christ freed us'. The Byzantine form is smoother, with the relative clause 'in which' and the 'then' placed first. The smoother reading is probably a scribe's tidying. The wording also fits the verses around it: 4:31 says 'we are free', and 5:1 states the purpose.
b: Some witnesses also move the 'therefore' or the word for 'free' in other ways, and the break between chapters 4 and 5 sits at different places in the manuscripts. The meaning of the verse does not change.

p: The KJV list begins 'Adultery, fornication'. The older text begins with 'sexual immorality'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: They are sexual immorality

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness')
readings.en: adultery, sexual immorality, uncleanness, shameless living
readings.plain: They are adultery, sexual immorality

why: The Plain follows the shorter list. 'Adultery' was easy to add: it is the first of the three sins in lists like Matthew 15:19 and 1 Corinthians 6:9, and a scribe might add it to fill out a familiar pattern. The oldest witnesses do not have it. Adultery is in any case included in 'sexual immorality' (porneia), a broad word.

p: The KJV list says 'envyings, murders, drunkenness'. The SBL and NA28 leave out 'murders'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort; Papyrus 46 (about AD 200) and Codex Vaticanus (300s) among the early manuscripts (Witness lists are those reported by Metzger and the NA28 apparatus; the individual manuscripts were not rechecked here.)
readings.plain: envy, drunkenness

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'envyings, murders, drunkenness')
readings.plain: envy, murders, drunkenness

why: The Plain follows the SBL and NA28, with the earliest witnesses. The case for 'murders' is real, though: the Greek words phthonoi ('envy') and phonoi ('murders') look and sound almost the same, so a scribe's eye could skip one by accident, and the Tyndale House editors decided that is what happened. The sense of the list does not depend on it, since murder is condemned elsewhere (Romans 1:29).
b: The pair is a play on sound in Greek (phthonoi, phonoi), which suggests that Paul may have written both.

p: Some editions read 'those of Christ Jesus', others 'those of Christ'. The NA28 prints 'Jesus' in brackets.

readings.w: SBLGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (witness lists not rechecked here)
readings.plain: Those who are Christ's

readings.w: NA28 (with 'Jesus' in brackets), NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: Those who are Christ Jesus's

why: The Plain follows the shorter form. The NA28 editors mark 'Jesus' as doubtful by printing it in brackets, and the editions are split. The meaning does not change. The manuscript support was not rechecked here.

a: If you do, you will fulfill
p: A one-letter difference makes the verb a promise or a command.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles
readings.plain: If you do, you will fulfill

readings.w: Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'and so fulfil the law of Christ')
readings.plain: In this way, fulfill

why: The Plain follows the future 'you will fulfill'. The two readings differ by one vowel, the future indicative anaplerosete against the aorist imperative anaplerosate. Both make sense: the future states the result of carrying each other's loads, the imperative restates the command. The manuscript support was not rechecked here; the editions split as shown, and the Byzantine text has the imperative. One possible reason for the imperative is that a scribe was drawn to the many commands around it (6:1-6), which would make the future the less obvious reading; that is an inference, not a reported fact.

p: One letter turns 'as we have opportunity' into 'while we may have opportunity'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
readings.plain: whenever we have the chance

readings.w: Westcott-Hort
readings.plain: whenever we may have the chance

why: The Plain follows the reading of nearly every edition. The difference is between an indicative and a subjunctive after hos, and the sense is almost the same: Paul urges them to do good while there is time.

a: The very ones who are having themselves circumcised
p: The tense of one word changes who Paul is describing: Gentiles taking circumcision now, or people already circumcised.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Textus Receptus
readings.plain: The very ones who are having themselves circumcised

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text (witness lists as reported by Metzger and the NA28 apparatus; the individual manuscripts were not rechecked here)
readings.plain: The very ones who have been circumcised

why: The Plain follows the present participle, which the SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles print. The perfect participle is printed by the Tyndale House GNT and is the Byzantine reading, and Metzger reports early manuscript support for it; that support was not rechecked here. The two readings point to different people. Present: people who are now being circumcised, or who take circumcision on, such as Gentile converts. Perfect: people who have already been circumcised, that is, Jews or earlier converts. The choice affects who the agitators were, but the sentence says the same thing about both groups: they do not keep the law. The note on this verse gives the debate. This is a close call.
b: This is one of the most discussed variants for deciding who the agitators were. If 'those having been circumcised', the agitators are Jews or Jewish converts. If 'those being circumcised', they may include Gentiles who have accepted circumcision (Munck).

a: Circumcision is nothing, and so is uncircumcision.
t: A short form and a longer one
p: The Byzantine text copies the wording of 5:6 here.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.orig: οὔτε γὰρ περιτομή τί ἐστιν οὔτε ἀκροβυστία
readings.en: For neither circumcision is anything nor uncircumcision
readings.plain: Circumcision is nothing, and so is uncircumcision.

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision')
readings.orig: ἐν γὰρ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ οὔτε περιτομή τι ἰσχύει, οὔτε ἀκροβυστία
readings.en: For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any strength nor uncircumcision
readings.plain: In Christ Jesus, circumcision has no strength, and neither does uncircumcision.

why: The Plain follows the shorter form. The Byzantine wording is almost exactly 5:6 ('In Christ Jesus, circumcision has no strength and neither does uncircumcision'), so a scribe may have copied it from there. The shorter, different form is also the one that fits the next clause, 'a new creation'.

p: A short title in the older text is longer in the Byzantine text.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.plain: carrying the marks of Jesus

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV: 'the marks of the Lord Jesus')
readings.en: the marks of the Lord Jesus
readings.plain: carrying the marks of the Lord Jesus

why: The Plain follows the shorter title, which the oldest editions have. Scribes liked fuller titles. Paul's plain 'Jesus' is what we might expect from him in speaking of the man who was crucified.

a: Brothers, may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.
p: The KJV letter ends with a line saying it was written from Rome. That line is a later addition.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text
readings.orig: μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοί· ἀμήν.
readings.plain: Brothers, may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

readings.w: Textus Receptus and some late manuscripts add a closing line (KJV: 'Unto the Galatians written from Rome')
readings.en: To the Galatians, written from Rome
readings.plain: Brothers, may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen. To the Galatians. Written from Rome.

why: The Plain stops at 'Amen'. The closing lines in some manuscripts are not Paul's. They are notes added by later copyists, and they differ from manuscript to manuscript. Rome is almost certainly wrong: Paul's own place of writing is not given in the letter, and the suggestions vary from Ephesus to Corinth to Antioch.
b: Such 'subscriptions' appear after most of Paul's letters in later manuscripts and are of little value as history. See also the introduction to the letter for the date and place of writing.
